strengths: Novel formulation of symmetry discovery as distribution learning over Lie groups, providing a unified framework for continuous and discrete symmetries
Thorough identification and analysis of 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon with solid theoretical justification via entropy analysis and posterior computation
Technically sound mathematical framework with correct derivations of target velocity fields and proper use of Lie group geometry (exponential/logarithm maps, orbit-stabilizer theorem)
Comprehensive experimental analysis on synthetic data with extensive visualizations and ablations demonstrating method behavior across different scenarios
Outperforms LieGAN baseline across all tested scenarios with substantially better Wasserstein-1 distances
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations including failure cases (icosahedral group) and open problems
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Experiments only on synthetic, noise-free point clouds; no validation on real-world data despite authors acknowledging 'scaling to noisy real-world datasets remains an open question'

CRITICAL: Method requires pre-specifying hypothesis group G, which is a substantial practical limitation that undermines the motivation for unsupervised symmetry discovery; no guidance provided for selecting G in practice
CRITICAL: Limited scalability—fails on icosahedral group (60 elements) even with proposed power schedule; works only for relatively small groups
The power schedule solution (n=5) appears ad-hoc without principled justification; no general method for selecting n for new problems
Method discovers closest group element in orbit rather than exact symmetries; while claimed as potentially advantageous for approximate symmetries, this is not validated
Limited baseline comparisons—only LieGAN tested; no quantitative comparison with Allingham et al. (2024) or Sherry & Smets (2025), making novelty claims difficult to substantiate

Novelty somewhat incremental over concurrent work (Sherry & Smets 2025) which independently developed flow matching on Lie groups; main difference is focus on symmetry discovery rather than methodological innovation
No demonstration of discovered symmetries in downstream applications (e.g., equivariant networks); practical utility remains unclear
Reproducibility concerns: no code provided, experiments only on synthetic data they generated, key hyperparameter choices not justified
Restricted scope: matrix Lie groups only, non-compact groups cause numerical challenges, limited to low-dimensional settings (SO(2), SO(3))

strengths: Novel formulation of symmetry discovery as distribution learning on Lie groups is elegant and enables unified treatment of continuous, discrete, and partially observed symmetries within a single framework without assuming fixed Lie algebra bases or specific distributions.

Identification of 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete groups is a valuable insight, well-documented through extensive empirical analysis (Appendix D) with clear evidence from entropy and posterior analysis. The proposed power schedule solution is practical and effective.

Strong empirical results substantially outperforming LieGAN on discrete symmetries (W₁: 0.072 vs 1.688 for C₄; 0.118 vs 1.861 for Ico) with comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning synthetic 2D/3D datasets, ModelNet10, partial symmetries, and robustness to masking.
Mathematically sound framework with detailed derivations (Appendix A). Clear presentation with good motivation, algorithmic descriptions, and extensive supporting visualizations throughout.
Handles multiple hypothesis groups (SO(2), GL(2,R)⁺, SO(3)) with flexibility in prior distributions, demonstrating that the approach is not tied to a specific parameterization.
weaknesses: Scalability and generality severely limited: only 128-point clouds evaluated; no demonstration on images, meshes, or high-dimensional data. Authors acknowledge 'small point clouds and limited number of objects,' undermining claims of broad applicability.

Still requires specifying hypothesis group G a priori; no principled guidance on selection in practice. Paper lacks analysis of: (1) performance degradation with misspecified G, (2) behavior when true symmetry H ⊄ G, (3) systematic selection criteria. This practical limitation is downplayed despite remaining a significant barrier.

Single baseline comparison (LieGAN only). Missing comparisons with Benton et al. (2020), Ko et al. (2024), Allingham et al. (2024) prevent understanding of relative performance and method applicability across settings.

Weak theoretical justification: intuition that 'inconsistent targets cancel' lacks formal proof; no convergence analysis or conditions for when method succeeds; claims about discovering 'approximate and partially observed' symmetries lack theoretical grounding.

Evaluation via Wasserstein-1 distance assumes known ground truth, making metrics unsuitable for truly unsupervised discovery. Circular dependency: requires ground truth to evaluate, yet claiming unsupervised discovery. Undermines evaluation for partial symmetry claims.

Partial symmetry claims overstated: formal treatment in Section 4.3 is thorough but experimental validation weak (one 2D example + robustness testing conflated with true partial discovery). Need clearer distinction.

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: power schedule parameter n set empirically to n=5 for one setting (SO(3)→Ico) with no evidence of transfer. GL(2)⁺ prior choice shows huge variance (W₁: 1.321 vs 0.428) but receives minimal discussion on selection guidance.
Last-minute convergence fix feels ad-hoc (manually tuned n=5 power schedule) rather than addressing root cause. Why not redesign loss or sampling more fundamentally?
Reproducibility concerns: code not mentioned as available; training dynamics (convergence epochs) missing; total training time not reported; some architectural choices appear arbitrary.
Missing critical ablations: only one problem setting for time schedule ablation; no systematic analysis of hypothesis group choice impact; limited exploration of architectural variations.

strengths: Novel reframing of symmetry discovery as distribution learning over Lie groups with principled mathematical foundation
Insightful identification and analysis of 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete symmetries with effective power time schedule solution
Unified framework handling continuous, discrete, approximate, and partially observed symmetries without fixed basis assumptions
Rigorous mathematical derivations with proper treatment of orbit-respecting interpolation paths and Lie group flow matching
Comprehensive experiments across 2D/3D synthetic and ModelNet10 datasets with appropriate evaluation metrics (Wasserstein-1 distance)
Significant empirical improvements over LieGAN baseline on discrete groups (e.g., SO(3)→Tet: 0.0885 vs 2.326)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations demonstrating the method and addressing key technical challenges
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope restricted to point clouds only; no evaluation on images, graphs, or other modalities despite motivation from diverse applications
Requires specifying hypothesis group G a priori without principled guidance for selection in new domains, limiting practical applicability
Incomplete baseline comparisons with only LieGAN tested; no comparisons with concurrent methods (Allingham et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2024)
Power time schedule parameter (n=5) determined empirically without theoretical justification; unclear if generalizes across different group structures and problem types
Scalability concerns unaddressed: no computational complexity analysis, no experiments on high-dimensional groups, unclear scaling with data size

No demonstration of downstream utility; evaluation focuses only on matching ground truth elements, not on whether discovered symmetries improve practical applications like equivariant network training
Limited ablation studies missing sensitivity analysis on metric choice, prior distribution, network architecture, and data conditioning robustness
Partial symmetry framework developed theoretically but only minimally explored experimentally (single Figure 2d example)
Implicit filtering mechanism relying on inconsistent training signals for non-symmetries lacks rigorous theoretical justification
Reproducibility gaps: no error bars/confidence intervals, unclear number of random seeds, no code availability mentioned, incomplete details despite appendices

strengths: Novel formulation of symmetry discovery as distribution learning on Lie groups via flow matching, enabling unified treatment of continuous and discrete symmetries without assuming fixed Lie algebra basis or coefficient distribution

Significant empirical improvements on discrete symmetry discovery (e.g., SO(3)→Ico: 0.104 vs 1.198 W₁ distance compared to LieGAN), with comprehensive experiments across synthetic 2D/3D, ModelNet10, and real-world MI-Motion datasets
Identification and effective solution of 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete groups through power time scheduling, with theoretical justification and ablation studies
Solid technical execution with sound mathematical foundations (Theorem B.4 with proof), careful derivations of flow field on Lie groups, and thorough appendices with proofs and additional experiments

Honest discussion of limitations (hypothesis group selection, identifiability under continuous stabilizers, numerical stability) with robustness analysis showing graceful degradation under noise and comprehensive ablation studies
weaknesses: Strong and restrictive theoretical assumptions (B.1-B.3) create significant gap between theory and practice: ideal convergence is unrealistic, globally generated support excludes partial symmetries, and point stabilizer conditions rule out objects with hidden symmetries, limiting practical applicability of Theorem B.4

Continuous stabilizer issue fundamentally unresolved: Appendix A acknowledges non-unique Lie algebra coordinates under continuous stabilizers, but only briefly discusses solutions (quotient formulations, auxiliary supervision) without exploration or empirical analysis of impact

Limited practical guidance on hypothesis group selection, which significantly affects performance (SO(2) much better than GL(2)⁺ in Table 1), leaving practitioners without principled methodology despite this being identified as a key limitation

Incremental improvements on continuous symmetries with comparable performance to baselines (RI ≈93-98%), limiting impact for primary use case; advantages primarily for specialized discrete symmetry discovery

Weak real-world evaluation: only one genuine real-world dataset (MI-Motion) with discovered C₄ symmetry already suggested by data description; no evaluation of whether discovered symmetries improve downstream tasks or validation against domain experts; no user studies
